title: source-coop CLI
text: The command line for Source Cooperative . Use it to: Get data credentials. Sign in through your browser once. AWS tools then get temporary S3 credentials for the Source Cooperative data proxy, and the CLI renews them when they expire. Manage source.coop. List, view, create, edit and delete products, members and service accounts. The source.coop API applies the same rules as the web UI. All commands work the same way: At a terminal, a command asks for the values that you do not give. -i shows records full screen, for you to move through. --json and the exit codes are stable, for scripts and AI agents. This guide is also a website, with a page for each section and docs for each release: https://source-cooperative.github.io/source-coop-cli/ . The demos in this guide use a stand-in for the API with made-up records ( demo-org , demo-user ). Their http://127.0.0.1:… URLs are local. Contents Install Quick start Signing in Reading data with AWS tools Managing products Managing members Managing service accounts Prompts Browsing with -i Scripts and AI agents Any API request Configuration Credential storage OIDC provider setup

title: Homebrew (macOS / Linux)
text: brew install source-cooperative/tap/source-coop

title: From GitHub Releases (recommended)
text: macOS / Linux: curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -LsSf \ https://github.com/source-cooperative/source-coop-cli/releases/latest/download/source-coop-cli-installer.sh | sh Windows PowerShell: powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://github.com/source-cooperative/source-coop-cli/releases/latest/download/source-coop-cli-installer.ps1 | iex"

title: From source
text: cargo install --git https://github.com/source-cooperative/source-coop-cli To see the installed version: source-coop --version

title: Shell completion
text: Add one of these lines to your shell's startup file: eval "$(source-coop completions bash)" # ~/.bashrc eval "$(source-coop completions zsh)" # ~/.zshrc, after compinit source-coop completions fish | source # ~/.config/fish/config.fish source-coop completions powershell | Out-String | Invoke-Expression # $PROFILE elvish is also available. TAB then completes commands, flags, flag values and record names: source-coop product view my-org/<TAB> shows the products of my-org . Before the / , it shows the accounts that you are a member of. source-coop service-account view my<TAB> shows full service account IDs, such as my-org--nightly-sync . It does not complete the ID of a new service account for create . How completion works: It always matches the installed version. On each TAB, the script runs source-coop with SOURCE_COOP_COMPLETE set. Names come from the API, as you. Completion uses your session's access token (or SOURCE_TOKEN ) and never renews it. When the token has expired, only public products complete. The next command that you run renews it. It reads the environment only. It uses SOURCE_API_URL and SOURCE_PROXY_URL . It ignores --api-url and --proxy-url on the command line. It waits 2 seconds for the API. After that, it shows no names, and bash shows file names. On macOS, the keychain can ask for your password. TAB waits up to one minute for you. Select Always Allow so that it does not ask again until you install a new build.

title: Quick start
text: source-coop auth login # sign in through your browser, once source-coop product list my-org # an account's products source-coop product create # asks for each value a new product needs aws s3 ls s3://my-org/my-data --profile source-coop # after you add the AWS profile (below) source-coop --help lists the commands. source-coop <command> --help lists the flags of a command, with examples.

title: Sign in
text: source-coop auth login This opens your browser. After you sign in, the CLI keeps the session in your OS keyring, or in a file if there is no keyring. The old name, source-coop login , also works. One session is used for all commands: creds exchanges the session's ID token at the data proxy for S3 credentials, for each role. Commands that use the source.coop API send the session's access token. The CLI renews expired tokens and credentials. You sign in again only when the session itself expires. Sign-in uses the OAuth2 Authorization Code flow with PKCE. The CLI then exchanges the OIDC ID token at the proxy's STS endpoint for temporary AWS credentials. Two flags change this: Without offline_access in --scope , the CLI cannot renew anything. You must sign in again when the credentials expire. With --no-cache , the CLI prints the credentials (in --format ) and keeps nothing.

title: Sign in on a remote server (no browser)
text: auth login receives the browser's redirect on a local port. On a server without a browser, forward that port over SSH: Connect with a port forward. Any free port is satisfactory; this example uses 8400 : ssh -L 8400:127.0.0.1:8400 user@server On the server, sign in on the forwarded port: source-coop auth login --port 8400 Open the URL that the CLI prints in your local browser, and sign in. The redirect to http://127.0.0.1:8400/callback goes through the tunnel to the CLI on the server. The session stays on the server (see File fallback ). source-coop creds renews the credentials there without a browser.

title: See your sign-in status
text: source-coop auth status Environment https://data.source.coop Login logged in Account Demo User (demo-user) Profile https://source.coop/demo-user Refresh token renewed 2026-10-13T14:00:00Z (3 hours ago); expires 2026-11-12 (in 29 days) ID token expires 2026-10-13T18:00:00Z (in 1 hour) Access token for https://source.coop, expires 2026-10-13T18:00:00Z (in 1 hour) Credentials _default: expire 2026-10-13T18:30:00Z (in 1 hour) auth status shows: If you are signed in, and the account. The CLI found the account when you signed in. A session from an older version does not have it, and auth status tells you to sign in again. When the cached tokens and the role's credentials expire. A profile link on the site of the session ( https://staging.source.coop for staging). It reads only the cache. It does not renew tokens or use the network. On a terminal, the session's state is green or red. When you must sign in again. The refresh token sets this. The CLI uses it to renew the other tokens and the credentials, so their expiry times do not matter. source.coop's identity provider (Ory) does not tell the CLI how long a refresh token lasts. Thus auth status shows: When the refresh token was last renewed. Each renewal starts its lifetime again. An estimate, to the day, of when it expires if not used. The estimate assumes 30 days, Ory's default. If the server uses a different lifetime, set SOURCE_REFRESH_TOKEN_LIFETIME (for example 720h or 14d ). This changes only the estimate. If the CLI cannot read the value, it ignores it and shows a warning. If a provider gives an expiry time, auth status shows that time. After that time, the session shows as expired. After only the estimate, it shows as likely expired (yellow), because the real lifetime can be longer. A session from an older version shows yes until its next renewal. With --json , auth status prints the same data: logged_in is false when the session has expired. It stays true when the session is only likely expired. Times are RFC 3339, each with an expired flag. The account includes its profile_url . If the provider gave no refresh-token expiry, estimated_lapse_at and the assumed_lifetime it uses are included. source-coop auth status --json | jq -r .login.refresh_token.issued_at auth status shows one environment and one role, because the keyring cannot list its entries. To see others, use --proxy-url and --role-arn (or SOURCE_PROXY_URL and SOURCE_ROLE_ARN ).

title: Use your session with other tools
text: auth token prints the session's access token for the source.coop API. If the token has expired, it renews it first. curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $(source-coop auth token)" https://source.coop/api/v1/... To send a request through the CLI, see Any API request .

title: Multiple environments (for example, staging)
text: Each proxy host is a different environment, with its own session and credentials. Thus you can be signed in to production and staging at the same time: source-coop auth login ( source .env.staging && source-coop auth login ) --proxy-url (or SOURCE_PROXY_URL ) selects the environment for all commands. The default is production. --api-url (or SOURCE_API_URL ) selects the site for commands that use the API. .env.staging sets both. An AWS profile for a different environment must use --proxy-url . If it does not, it gets production credentials: [profile source-coop] credential_process = source-coop creds endpoint_url = https://data.source.coop [profile source-coop-staging] credential_process = source-coop creds --proxy-url https://data.staging.source.coop endpoint_url = https://data.staging.source.coop

title: Sign out
text: auth logout removes the session of one environment and the credentials of one role. It removes them from the keyring and from the file fallback . source-coop auth logout source-coop auth logout --proxy-url https://data.staging.source.coop --role-arn reader-role source-coop auth logout --json # {"proxy_url": …, "role_arn": …, "removed": {"session": true, "credentials": true}} It uses --proxy-url ( SOURCE_PROXY_URL ) and --role-arn ( SOURCE_ROLE_ARN ), as creds does. The keyring cannot list its entries, so the credentials of other roles stay. You can use them until they expire, but the CLI cannot renew them without the session. To remove them now, run auth logout --role-arn <role> for each role. auth logout does not revoke tokens at the identity provider.

title: Sign-in options
text: Flag Env var Default Description --issuer SOURCE_OIDC_ISSUER https://auth.source.coop OIDC issuer URL --client-id SOURCE_OIDC_CLIENT_ID 197e20e7-... OAuth2 client ID --proxy-url SOURCE_PROXY_URL https://data.source.coop S3 proxy URL for STS. Also selects the environment of the session. --role-arn SOURCE_ROLE_ARN _default Role ARN to assume --format credential-process Output format: credential-process , env or aws-credentials --profile source-coop Profile name for --format aws-credentials --duration Session duration, for example 3600 , 90s , 5m , 12h , 1d (a number alone is seconds) --scope openid offline_access OAuth2 scopes. offline_access lets creds renew credentials. --audience SOURCE_API_AUDIENCE https://source.coop Audience of the API access token. If empty, the CLI requests none, and only creds works. --port 0 (random) Local callback port --no-cache Print the credentials and keep nothing

title: AWS credential_process
text: Sign in once: source-coop auth login Add a profile to ~/.aws/config : [profile source-coop] credential_process = source-coop creds endpoint_url = https://data.source.coop Use AWS tools with that profile: aws s3 ls s3://my-account/my-product --profile source-coop When the credentials expire, source-coop creds gets new ones with the session. Run source-coop auth login again only if this fails, for example because the refresh token expired or was revoked.

title: Output formats
text: creds and auth login print credentials in one of three formats. Select one with --format : credential-process (default): JSON for AWS credential_process . source-coop creds env : shell export statements. They set AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID , AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY and AWS_SESSION_TOKEN in your shell. eval $(source-coop creds --format env) aws-credentials : an INI profile for ~/.aws/credentials . --profile sets the section name. source-coop creds --format aws-credentials >> ~/.aws/credentials [source-coop] # expires 2026-07-13T12:00:00Z aws_access_key_id = ... aws_secret_access_key = ... aws_session_token = ... Tip These credentials are temporary. When they expire, run the command again. Each run adds a new section, and AWS uses the last one, so remove old sections occasionally. We recommend credential_process in ~/.aws/config instead.

title: Multiple roles
text: Warning The Source Cooperative data proxy does not yet support custom roles. The CLI keeps the credentials of each role separately: source-coop auth login --role-arn reader-role source-coop auth login --role-arn admin-role Use --role-arn with creds to select the role: [profile source-coop] credential_process = source-coop creds --role-arn reader-role endpoint_url = https://data.source.coop [profile source-coop-admin] credential_process = source-coop creds --role-arn admin-role endpoint_url = https://data.source.coop

title: Managing products
text: source-coop product lists, views, creates, edits and deletes products through the source.coop API ( /api/v1 ). The CLI does not check values itself. It shows the API's errors for each field. A product's name is ACCOUNT/PRODUCT .

title: List and view
text: source-coop product list # public products source-coop product list my-org --json # the products of one account, as JSON source-coop product list --format table # one row for each product; tab-separated when piped source-coop product list -q climate # search titles, descriptions and IDs source-coop product list --tags zarr,climate --featured # featured products with all these tags source-coop product list -L 100 # up to 100 (default 30, or all in the pager) source-coop product list my-org -i # move through them full screen (see "Browsing with -i") source-coop product view my-org/my-product # one product source-coop product view my-org/my-product -w # open its page in the browser source-coop product view my-org/my-product -i # its screen, with shortcuts; with no name, select one first list has two formats: --format details (default) shows the fields of each product, as view does. --format table shows one row for each product. On a terminal, the table is aligned and has a header. When piped, the rows are tab-separated, with no header. On a terminal, list shows the products in your pager and gets more pages as you read. In other cases, it stops at --limit . To continue from there, give --cursor the cursor that the last list printed.

title: Create
text: source-coop product create # asks for all values source-coop product create my-org/my-product # asks for the other values source-coop product create my-org/my-product -t "My product" -d "What's in it" \ --visibility public --data-connection my-connection echo '{"title": "My product"}' | source-coop product create my-org/my-product -F - Give the values as flags ( --title , --description , --visibility , --data-connection ), as a JSON object with --from-file PATH ( - for stdin), or both. Flags take priority. At a terminal, create asks for the missing values, with the web form's defaults: The accounts that you can create products in. A title made from the product ID. The data connections that the account can use. The visibilities that the selected data connection allows. You cannot change a product's data connection after you create it. For how to go back, the review, and drafts, see Prompts . create prints the product's URL on stdout and its message on stderr. Thus url=$(source-coop product create ...) works.

title: Edit
text: source-coop product edit my-org/my-product # a form of its fields source-coop product edit my-org/my-product --visibility unlisted source-coop product edit my-org/my-product -d "New description" --json source-coop product edit my-org/my-product --disable # --enable makes it active again (admins only) source-coop product edit -i # select one of your account's products edit uses the same values as create , but not the data connection. Give them as flags or with --from-file . --disable and --enable are flags only. edit prints the product's URL on stdout. With no flags, edit opens a full-screen form of the title, description and visibility: ↑/↓ moves between the fields. Enter changes the selected field, starting from its current value. Esc keeps the value. The form shows only the visibilities that the data connection allows. A changed field shows its old value. s , or Enter on Save changes , shows the changes and asks you to confirm. ← goes back to the form. Esc or ← on the form cancels. If you changed a field, the form asks first.

title: Delete
text: source-coop product delete my-org/my-product # asks you to type the name source-coop product delete my-org/my-product --preserve-data # keep its objects in storage source-coop product delete my-org/my-product --yes --json # no questions, for scripts source-coop product delete -i # select one of your account's products delete asks two questions: Keep the product's data in storage? --preserve-data answers yes. Type the product's name. If the text is different, nothing is deleted. Without a terminal, delete needs --yes .

title: Managing members
text: source-coop member manages the members of an organization ( ACCOUNT ) or a product ( ACCOUNT/PRODUCT ). source-coop invitation answers the invitations that you receive. A member's name is their account ID. You cannot invite by email. source-coop member list my-org # members and open invitations source-coop member list my-org/my-data --json # the members of a product, as JSON source-coop member list my-org --state invited # only open invitations source-coop member list my-org -i # move through the members full screen source-coop member view my-org alice # one member; -i for its screen source-coop member invite my-org alice bob --role maintainers source-coop member invite my-org/my-data -A people.txt --role read_data source-coop member invite my-org # asks who to invite, and the role source-coop member edit my-org alice --role owners source-coop member edit my-org -i # select a member, then a role source-coop member revoke my-org alice # also withdraws an open invitation source-coop member leave my-org # end your own membership With shell completion , TAB shows: For ACCOUNT or ACCOUNT/PRODUCT : your organizations and their products. For a member: the members of that organization or product. For invite : the organization's members who are not yet members of the product. For invitation accept , reject and member leave : your invitations and memberships. Roles , from most to least access: owners , maintainers , write_data , read_data . Only owners can make a member an owner, or change or revoke an owner. Owners and maintainers can manage the other roles. A product's member list shows only the product's own members. The organization's members can also use its products, and show in the organization's list. invite takes account IDs as arguments. --accounts-file PATH ( -A , - for stdin) adds one ID from each line. It skips empty lines and lines that start with # . --from-file reads account_id and role from a JSON object. Each account gets its own invitation. If the API refuses one, the CLI shows the error and sends the others. Then the command fails. At a terminal, invite asks for the missing accounts and role, and then asks you to confirm. The default role is read_data . It shows owners only if you can give that role. ← goes back one question. If invitations fail, the CLI saves the ones not sent as a draft. The next invite to the same place offers them again. If you invite a service account of the product's owner, it becomes a member at once. Its role must be read_data or write_data . edit without --role asks for a role, starting from the current one. You cannot change the role of an invitation. Revoke it and invite again. revoke asks you to confirm. For your own membership, you must also type the organization or product name. leave always asks you to type the name, because only an owner or maintainer can add you again. Without a terminal, revoke and leave need --yes . With --json , these commands print the memberships as the API gives them: membership_id , account_id , membership_account_id , product_id (for a product), role , state and state_changed . invite --json prints an array of the new memberships. create and delete are other names for invite and revoke . member list -i uses the same keys as product list -i . On a member's screen: e changes the role. d revokes the membership. For an invitation, d withdraws it, and e is not available. b opens their profile.

title: Your invitations
text: source-coop invitation list # invitations that wait for your answer source-coop invitation list -i # open one, then accept (a) or reject (r) it source-coop invitation accept my-org/my-data source-coop invitation reject my-org source-coop invitation accept -i # select an invitation When you accept, you become a member with the role of the invitation. With --json , the command prints the membership after the change.

title: Managing service accounts
text: A service account is an account for software, such as a GitHub Actions workflow or a script with an API key. It has an owner: you, or an organization that you own or maintain. source.coop must first let that account own service accounts. A service account's ID is the owner's ID, then -- , then its own name: my-org--nightly-sync . AWS tools use this ID: role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::my-org--nightly-sync:role/FullAccess . source-coop service-account shows a service account as the web UI does: what it is, how it signs in, and the products it can use. source-coop service-account list my-org # my-org's service accounts (yours, with no owner) source-coop service-account list my-org --no-pager # print directly, not in the pager source-coop service-account list my-org -i # move through them full screen (keys as for products) source-coop service-account view my-org--nightly-sync # --json adds `trusts`, `keys` and `memberships` source-coop service-account view my-org--nightly-sync -w # open its page in the browser source-coop service-account create # asks for all values, as the web form does source-coop service-account create my-org--nightly-sync --name "Nightly sync" \ --github my-org/data --branch main --access my-org/my-data=write source-coop service-account edit my-org--nightly-sync --name "Nightly sync" source-coop service-account edit my-org--nightly-sync # a form of its name and products source-coop service-account edit my-org--nightly-sync --disable # --enable lets it sign in again source-coop service-account delete my-org--nightly-sync # asks you to type its ID create takes values as flags, as a JSON object with --from-file , or both: Flags: --name , one --github workflow, a --key with --expires and --out , and --access (one or more). JSON uses the API's fields: name , local_id , github_subjects , key , grants . At a terminal, create asks for the missing values: the owner, the name, the ID (made from the name), workflows and an API key, and products. Then it shows all values, with the condition that each workflow must match, and asks you to confirm. If create issues a key, it gives you the key as sign-in add does. But stdout gets the account's ID, not the key. To keep the key, use --out or --json . create and edit print the service account's ID on stdout. Thus id=$(source-coop service-account create …) works. Going back, drafts, the sign-in check and --yes work as for products. edit --disable stops all sign-ins as the service account. It keeps its sign-ins and products. --enable lets its workflows and its keys that are not revoked sign in again. delete removes the service account, its sign-ins and its access to products. Type its ID to confirm, or use --yes .

title: Sign-ins
text: A service account signs in in one of two ways: A GitHub Actions workflow that it trusts. The trust is for one repository and one branch, tag or environment. GitHub vouches for each run, so there is no secret to keep. An API key , where GitHub is not available. source-coop service-account sign-in add my-org--nightly-sync --github my-org/data --branch main source-coop service-account sign-in add my-org--nightly-sync --github my-org/data --environment production source-coop service-account sign-in add my-org--nightly-sync --subject repo:my-org/data:ref:refs/tags/v1 source-coop service-account sign-in remove my-org--nightly-sync repo:my-org/data:ref:refs/heads/main source-coop service-account sign-in remove my-org--nightly-sync -i # select a sign-in --github OWNER/REPO with --branch , --tag or --environment makes the subject that GitHub's tokens contain, such as repo:OWNER/REPO:ref:refs/heads/main . --subject takes a subject as it is. The CLI asks GitHub how the repository's tokens name it, as the web UI does. Some repositories use IDs ( owner@123/repo@456 ), which never match owner/repo . For a private repository, set GH_TOKEN (or GITHUB_TOKEN ). If GitHub does not answer, the CLI tells you how to find the name. At a terminal, without these flags, sign-in add asks for the repository and the runs to trust. Then it shows the condition and asks you to confirm. API keys are for places without GitHub's tokens, such as a cron job on a cluster. Each key has a label that tells where it is used. Use it to find the key to revoke. A key expires after 30 days, 90 days (default), one year, never, or on a date (at midnight UTC). source-coop service-account sign-in add my-org--nightly-sync --key "HPC cron job" --expires 1y --out ~/.source-coop/nightly.key key=$(source-coop service-account sign-in add my-org--nightly-sync --key "HPC cron job") # piped: only the key on stdout source-coop service-account sign-in edit my-org--nightly-sync key:a1B2c3 --expires never # a new expiry, from now source-coop service-account sign-in remove my-org--nightly-sync key:a1B2c3 # revoke it; asks you to type key:a1B2c3 The CLI shows a key one time only, when it issues the key: --out PATH writes the key to a new file that only you can read. AWS tools read the key from a file. If a file is already at that path, the CLI does not overwrite it. It shows the key. It also shows the key if it cannot write the file. When piped, stdout gets only the key. On a terminal, the CLI asks for a file name. Press Enter to show the key instead. view lists each key by its label and its last six characters, such as key:a1B2c3 . sign-in edit and sign-in remove use this name. view also shows when the key was last used and when it expires. It shows revoked and expired keys dimmed. You cannot restore a revoked key. At a terminal, without flags, sign-in add asks if you want a workflow or a key. sign-in edit -i and sign-in remove -i let you select one. If a key leaks, anyone with the key can revoke it, without signing in. The command reads the key from stdin, so the key is not in your shell history: source-coop service-account sign-in revoke-key < leaked-key-file

title: Access to products
text: A service account can read, or read and write, its owner's products. Each grant is a usual membership of the product. create --access gives access when you create the service account. edit --access gives access, changes the role, or removes access ( =none ). source-coop service-account edit my-org--nightly-sync --access my-org/my-data=write --access my-org/old-data=none If the product already has that role, or has no access to remove, nothing changes. Thus you can run an edit two times safely. With no flags, edit opens a full-screen form with Name , then the products under Can reach , each with its role: ↑/↓ moves. Enter changes the selected row: the name, or the access to a product (Read, Read and write, or No access). Grant a product… adds one of the owner's other products. A changed row shows its old value. s , or Enter on Save changes , shows the changes and asks you to confirm. ← goes back to the form. Esc or ← on the form cancels. If you changed a row, the form asks first. --disable and --enable are flags only.

title: Use a service account
text: Workflows and scripts sign in with standard AWS tools, not with this CLI. usage prints what they need, as the web UI does: source-coop service-account usage my-org--nightly-sync --subject repo:my-org/data:ref:refs/heads/main \ > .github/workflows/source-coop.yml # a workflow that uses aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials source-coop service-account usage my-org--nightly-sync --key # the AWS_* variables for a key in a file At a terminal, without --subject or --key , usage asks which sign-in to show.

title: Prompts
text: At a terminal, commands that change data ask for the values that you do not give. All commands ask in the same way. Priority. Flags take priority over --from-file PATH ( -F , - for stdin). The file takes priority over prompts. The CLI asks only for the missing values. Sign-in check. Before the first question, create , edit and delete make sure that you are signed in. Go back. To go back to the previous question, press ↑ in a text question (or ← at the start of the line), or ← in a list. The previous answer stays as the start value. Later answers stay. The CLI skips questions that a flag or file answered. Review. After it asks a question, the command shows what it will send and asks you to confirm. ← goes back. Long text. Type a description on one line, or press Ctrl+E to write it in your editor ( $VISUAL or $EDITOR ). A one-line description shows in the line for you to edit. An empty line removes it. A longer description is not shown in the line. Press Enter on the empty line to keep it. Errors. If the API refuses a value, the CLI shows the reason and asks for that value again. Cancel. Press Esc (or q in a list). The CLI shows "Cancelled; nothing was changed." and exits with code 1. When you must type a name to confirm, Enter on an empty line also cancels. Ctrl+C stops at once, with exit code 130. Drafts. If the send fails (for example, no connection, an expired session or a server error), the CLI saves your answers as a draft. Run the same command again to use them. Flags take priority over the draft. You can also give the draft file with --from-file . After a successful send, the CLI deletes the draft. Drafts are in your OS's application state folder: Platform Path Linux ~/.local/state/source-coop/drafts ( $XDG_STATE_HOME ) macOS ~/Library/Application Support/source-coop/drafts Windows %LocalAppData%\source-coop\drafts The CLI does not ask questions if stdin or stderr is not a terminal, or if SOURCE_PROMPT_DISABLED is set. It sends the values that it has, and the API tells you which ones are missing. Then delete, revoke and leave need --yes .

title: Browsing with -i
text: -i ( --interactive ) is available where a command names or lists records: list -i shows the records full screen. view -i shows the screen of one record. edit , delete , revoke and the other commands let you select the record if you do not name it. -i uses the full terminal. When you exit, the terminal is as before. Results show as a notice on the screen. Key In a list On a record ↑ ↓ ( k j ), PgUp PgDn, Home End move → Enter ( l ) open the record ← Esc ( h q ) exit (in search results: go back to the full list) go back to the list / filter the loaded records by text, with the number of matches (Esc clears the filter). In all public products, Enter searches the server, and ← exits the results. b open in the browser open in the browser e edit (for a member: change the role) d delete (for a member: revoke) a r accept or reject (an invitation) To edit or delete, you must open the record first. Thus a wrong key in a list changes nothing. The shortcuts do the same as the commands, with the same questions. Lists get more records as you move down.

title: Scripts and AI agents
text: source-coop --help ends with a summary of this section. The --help of each command shows its flags and examples. Thus an AI agent can learn the CLI from the CLI.

title: Output
text: Data goes to stdout. Messages go to stderr. Thus url=$(source-coop product create ...) works. On a terminal, output is for people. It has color, unless NO_COLOR is set or CLICOLOR=0 . Lists show in your pager: $SOURCE_PAGER , $PAGER , then less -FRX . --no-pager or SOURCE_PAGER=cat prints directly. When piped, output is plain , with no pager. -v ( --verbose ) prints the HTTP requests and responses on stderr.

title: JSON
text: These commands accept --json : auth status and auth logout . product list , view , create , edit and delete . All member and invitation commands. service-account list , view , create , edit and delete , and sign-in add , edit and remove . Commands that change data print the record after the change. service-account edit --json prints the account as view --json does. With --json : stdout contains one JSON document and nothing else. Notes and progress go to stderr. Field names are the API's. Times are RFC 3339. New fields can be added. Fields are not renamed or removed. These commands do not accept --json , because their output is already for machines: creds ( --format ), auth token (a token), api (the API's response), completions (a shell script) and service-account usage (a workflow or shell exports). auth login does not accept it either, because it uses the browser. Use auth status --json after it. With --json , an error is also JSON, on stderr. If the error came from the API, it contains the data of the API's RFC 9457 problem: code and status . type : a URL to a page that explains the error and what to do. request_id : give it if you report the error. field_errors : if the API refused the input, the fields to correct, by path ( metadata.title ). {"error": {"code": "invalid", "message": "…", "status": 400, "field_errors": {"title": ["…"]}, "type": "https://source.coop/api/problems/invalid", "request_id": "…"}}

title: Exit codes
text: All commands use the same exit codes: Code Meaning 0 Success 1 Other failure, including a cancelled prompt 2 Incorrect command-line usage 3 The API refused the input (HTTP 400, 409, 422). Correct the named fields and try again. 4 Not signed in, or not allowed (HTTP 401, 403) 5 Not found (HTTP 404) 130 Interrupted (Ctrl+C)

title: Use the API without signing in
text: If SOURCE_TOKEN is set, the CLI sends it to the API instead of the session's access token. Thus a script or CI job can use the API without auth login .

title: Any API request
text: source-coop api sends a request to /api/v1 as you, and prints the response. Use it for what the other commands do not do. source-coop api products/my-org -q limit=5 source-coop api products/my-org -f product_id=new -f title="New" -f description="" \ -f visibility=public -f data_connection_id=my-connection source-coop api products/my-org/new -X PATCH -F changes.json -f title="Renamed" echo '{"title": "Renamed", "tags": ["a"]}' | source-coop api products/my-org/new -X PATCH -F - Flag Does -q key=value Adds a query parameter. -f key=value Sets a field in the JSON body. A value that is valid JSON ( 5 , true , null , ["a","b"] ) is sent as JSON. Other values are strings. To send a JSON-like value as a string, quote it: -f product_id='"2024"' . -F file.json Reads the body from a file ( - for stdin). -f fields replace its keys. -X METHOD Sets the method. The default is GET , or POST with a body. A GET has no body. The path is always under /api/v1 . A query string in the path is kept. The API's OpenAPI spec at https://source.coop/api/openapi lists the paths and their fields. api prints the response body on stdout as the API sent it, so it does not accept --json . It also prints error responses there. If the status is not a success, the exit code shows the type of error (see Exit codes ). Public data needs no sign-in. Other requests use the session from source-coop auth login , with an access token for the API ( --audience , default https://source.coop ). The CLI renews this token when necessary. If SOURCE_TOKEN is set, the CLI sends it instead. To use a different deployment, such as http://localhost:3000 , set --api-url (or SOURCE_API_URL ).

title: Configuration
text: The CLI has no configuration file. Flags and environment variables set all values. A flag takes priority over its variable. Env var Flag Default Sets SOURCE_PROXY_URL --proxy-url https://data.source.coop The environment: the data proxy, and the session and credentials to use SOURCE_API_URL --api-url https://source.coop The source.coop site whose API ( /api/v1 ) commands use SOURCE_TOKEN A bearer token for the API, used instead of the session's SOURCE_ROLE_ARN --role-arn _default The role for creds , auth login , status and logout SOURCE_OIDC_ISSUER --issuer https://auth.source.coop Where auth login signs in SOURCE_OIDC_CLIENT_ID --client-id source.coop's The OAuth2 client for auth login SOURCE_API_AUDIENCE --audience https://source.coop The audience of the API access token that auth login requests SOURCE_REFRESH_TOKEN_LIFETIME 30d The refresh-token lifetime that auth status assumes, for example 720h or 14d SOURCE_PROMPT_DISABLED If set to any value, the CLI never asks questions SOURCE_PAGER , PAGER --no-pager less -FRX The pager for lists on a terminal VISUAL , EDITOR The editor that Ctrl+E opens for long text GH_TOKEN , GITHUB_TOKEN Lets the CLI ask GitHub about the workflows of a private repository NO_COLOR , CLICOLOR=0 No color, also on a terminal .env.staging in this repository sets the values for staging. Run source .env.staging before a command, or use a subshell as in Multiple environments .

title: Credential storage
text: The CLI keeps the session (the Ory refresh, ID and access tokens) and the temporary STS credentials of each role. Thus creds and the API commands work without a new sign-in. Only the session keeps the refresh token. The refresh token changes each time it is used. Thus all roles and all API calls renew through the session, one at a time.

title: OS keyring (default)
text: The CLI keeps credentials in the OS keyring, with the service name source-coop-cli : The key of each role's credentials is its role ARN, for example _default . The key of the session is @session . For environments other than production, both keys start with the proxy host, for example data.staging.source.coop/_default and data.staging.source.coop/@session . Platform Backend macOS Keychain ( security / Keychain Access) Windows Credential Manager Linux Secret Service API (GNOME Keyring, KDE Wallet) via D-Bus

title: File fallback
text: If there is no OS keyring (for example on servers, in containers and in CI), the CLI uses JSON files in the OS cache folder. On Unix, the files have 0600 permissions. You do not need to configure this. Platform Path macOS ~/Library/Caches/source-coop/credentials/<role>.json Linux ~/.cache/source-coop/credentials/<role>.json Windows %LocalAppData%\source-coop\credentials\<role>.json The session is in source-coop/session.json . Other environments use the same layout in source-coop/env/<host>/ , or in source-coop/env/<host>/<port>/ if the port is not the default. For example: source-coop/env/data.staging.source.coop/session.json .

title: OIDC provider setup
text: The CLI uses the OAuth2 Authorization Code flow with PKCE. It starts a temporary local server at http://127.0.0.1:{port}/callback to receive the authorization code. The OAuth2 client must have a redirect URI that agrees with this. Use one of these two options.

title: Option A: Allow all ports (recommended)
text: Register http://127.0.0.1/callback as a redirect URI on the OAuth2 client. RFC 8252 Section 7.3 says that loopback redirect URIs must allow all ports. Ory Network does this: a URI without a port allows all ports. The CLI's default, --port 0 , uses a random free port. This works with option A.

title: Option B: One fixed port
text: Register a redirect URI with a port, for example http://127.0.0.1:8400/callback . Then run the CLI with that port: source-coop auth login --role-arn <ARN> --port 8400

title: Client configuration
text: Configure the OAuth2 client as a public client (no client secret): Grant type : Authorization Code Token endpoint auth method : none (PKCE replaces the secret) Allowed scopes : openid , offline_access Redirect URIs : http://127.0.0.1/callback (see above) Allowed audiences : the source.coop site of the API ( https://source.coop or https://staging.source.coop ). Without it, Ory refuses a sign-in that requests that audience. Access token strategy : jwt . Then the API can verify access tokens with Ory's public keys, and does not need to ask Ory about each token.
